# Data Engineering

## Diet data: <br> National Food Survey <br> (1974 to 2000)

All dietary data for this project originates from the UK government's National Food Suvery (NFS). The NFS started in 1940 and eventually evolved into the Living Costs and Food Survey, which is active in 2026. 

However, not all of the associated data is publicly available.

For interested parties with institutional credentials, the [UK Data Service](https://ukdataservice.ac.uk) does provide a curated batch of NFS data that spans from 1974-2000.  

Each year, approximately 7,000 households across the UK were chosen at random from voting roles and asked to participate by keeping a one week diet diary. From 1974 to 2000, almost 190,000 households participated. 

Consenting households tracked all food purchases for one week, recording the consumable quantity ('cq') of each purchase and assigning it to one of over 300 minor food codes ('minfd'). Each minor food codeh can be mapped to one of 184 major food codes ('majfd').  

There are several native food group mappings included with the NFS data, but those food groupings tend to focus on economic details more than nutrition oriented details.  So, this study assigned each row in the diet diary to one of sixteen food groups based on an iterative literature informed (CITATIONS) manual review of all reported foods. This food group mapping is included in the Appendix.

Additionally, the NFS included annually adjusted nutrient conversion information for each of the minor food codes, allowing the recorded type and quantity to be converted into a nutrient profile for that purchase, and aggregated to a nutrient profile for each household.

Demographic and economic information is also included with the NFS data. However, this analysis assesses diet composition per calorie, not diet quantity per capita.  So, the only demographic information that was ultimately used in this analysis is the regional location of each household.


### Dietary Data Feature Engineering

#### Household food group profiles

For each diet diary row, calories were calculated based on NFS provided nutrient conversion factor for Energy (kCal) for the given food multiplied by the consumable quantity (cq) reported, as depicted in @eq-row-calories

$$
calories_{row} = cq_{row} \times \text{energy conversion factor}_{row}
$$ {#eq-row-calories}

 
Then, for each household, calories were aggregated for each of the assigned food groups, and then divided by total calories for that household.

$$
{calorie_ratio}_{food group} = \frac{\text{total calories per food group}}{\text{total calories per household}}
$$ {#eq-food-groups-calorie-ratio}


This resulted in a 'calorie ratio' for each food group for that household for that week.  This normalized metric cancels out quantity, and purely examines the qualitative composition of each household's reported food acquisition for the week.  Therefore, the number of people in the household do not factor into this metric, and further demographic considerations did not need to be calculated.

Finally, calorie ratios for all food groups were normalized by Standard Scaler and z-scored, with the means set to zero and the standard deviations set to plus or minus one.

#### Household nutrient profiles

Total calories were calculated for each household as with the food group feature engineering (Eq 1).  Then, each minor food code 'minfd' was converted to the nutrient profile for that food multipled by the quantity reported. This effectively expanded each diary entry row into twenty rows, one for each of the twenty nutrients tracked throughout the data, with the appropriate unit quantity for each nutrient reported.  



$$
calories_{row} = cq_{row} \times \text{energy conversion factor}_{row}
$$ {#eq-food-groups-calorie-ratio-3}

 Maintaining each nutrient's native unit (grams, milligrams, micrograms, etc), the total quantity of each nutrient across all food purchases was aggregated for each household. Those quantities were then divided by total calories for that household.

$$
calories_{row} = cq_{row} \times \text{energy conversion factor}_{row}
$$ {#eq-food-groups-calorie-ratio-4}

The resultant nutrient profile metric, 'quantity per total calories,' is similar in spirit to the 'calorie-ratio' metric from the food groups. 

However, a pure calorie comparison for nutrients would not be viable, as certain nutrients (carbohydrates, fats) have abundant calories while other nutrients (vitamins) have essentially zero calories. Hence, native nutrient units were maintained and divided by the common total calories.  This might preclude comparison amongst nutrients, but this analysis assesses household nutrient profiles, so the variation in fundamental units was not problematic.

Furthermore, variations in magnitude amongst the derived nutrient-quanity-per-total-calorie unit was also subjected to the Standared Scaler and z-scored before analysis.


## Disease data: <br> Global Burden of Disease <br> (1990 to 2023)

Population-level disease risk rates for High LDL cholesterol and other metabolic-disease associated risk factors were acquired from the Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation (IHME), using their Global Burden of Disease (GBD) Results tool (https://vizhub.healthdata.org/gbd-results/).

The data was specifically selected from this open API to find the summary exposure value (SEV) risk rates.  The IHME defines SEV as "A measure of a population’s exposure to a risk factor that takes into account the extent of exposure by risk level and the severity of that risk’s contribution to disease burden." https://www.healthdata.org/sites/default/files/files/policy_report/GBD/2016/IHME_GBD2015_Report_Glossary-of-terms_2016.pdf

Other metics such as disability-adjusted life years (DALYs) or simple mortality rates would be confounded by chronic disease management and treatment: society developing better medical management of chronic diseases might decrease mortality rates from associated risk factors, even if the prevelance of the risk factor is increasing. SEV was the best available metric from the GBD results tool to assess risk factor prevelance.  From there, the chronic disease risk factors and conditions for which SEV information were metabolic risks: High LDL Cholesterol, High Body Mass Index, High Fasting Plasma Glucose Systolic Blood Pressure, Kidney Dysfunction, Low Bone Mineral Density, and overall Metabolic Risks. 

These risk rates were obtained preaggreagted at a population level, grouped by UK region and by year.

## Pipeline

### Diet data cleaning

The NFS evolved over time, and this evolution prompted several data cleaning decisions for this analysis.  

To start, alcohol, confectioneries, and soft drinks were added as reportable food options in 1992. Previous to 1992, it is presumed that some UK households did purchase alochol, confectioneries, and soft drinks though the records cannot show this.  All three of these are considered high calorie, so their sudden appearance does skew calorie adjusted calculations. In order to maintain consistency over time, all diet diary rows from these three categories were dropped from analysis, though the related households and all their other diet diary entries were retained.

Initial analysis before dropping alochol had desiginated alochol as its own food group, for 17 total food groups.  After dropping all alochol rows, this analysis looked at 16 total foodgroups, as depicted in the Heatmaps in Figs X and Y.

Northern Ireland was only included in the survey starting in 1996. So, in the interest of consistency, Northern Ireland households were excluded from this analysis altogether.

The nutrient conversion information evolved over time as well, tracking 21 nutrients in 1974 and over 40 nutrients by 2000.  As with pruning rows from late-added foods and locations, nutrient trends were only assessed for the nutrients that were tracked throughout the entire dataset.  One of the included nutrients was Energy in megaJoules (MJ), which was collinear with Energy in kCal, so Energy in MJ was also dropped from nutrient analysis, resulting in 20 assessed nutrients.

The NSF and IHME data have a discrepancy in UK government office regions as well: the 1974 to 2000 NFS data list Merseyside as a distinct region, while the 1990 to 2023 IHME data includes that some geographical area as part of North West England.  So, before aggregation, all NFS households from Merseyside were reassigned as being part of North West England, for consistency between datasets.

A final cleaning step was to prune households that reported a physiologically unrealistic amount of calories, below a threshold that people require to live.  These households were considered to have provided unreliable data and were excluded from analysis.  The caloric floor threshold was set to two standard deviations below the mean of log-space per capita calorie intake, inspired by similar approaches in the literature [REFERENCE].  While the overall analysis does not rely on per capita calculations, this pruning step does. Per capita per household calculations were adjusted for age and sex (adult males = 1, adult females = 0.8, children = 0.5, elderly adults = 0.85), consistent with the literature [REFERENCE].

### Diet data aggregation

Dietary data aggregation was undertaken to generate the features described with @eq-food-groups-calorie-ratio, @eq-row-calories, @eq-food-groups-calorie-ratio-3, and @eq-food-groups-calorie-ratio-4 above.
The raw download from the UK Data Service has a folder for each year between 1974 and 2000, with space separated text files for diet diary, household information, and nutrient conversion factors.  All years of the NFS data share minor to major food code look up tables with consistent food code descriptions.


### Household food group profile aggregation

Year by year, calories nutrient conversion information (Energy kCal) was joined to each row of the diet diary (on minor food code, 'minfd'), multiplied by consumable quantity 'cq', and then summed by household to calculate total calories for that household (@eq-row-calories). Total household calories was later joined back to un-aggregated data as needed.

Minor food codes were mapped to major food codes, which were then mapped to custom food group labels (see Appendix).  Then each row was grouped by household and by foodgroup, aggregating total calories for each food group and for each household.  From there, everyhouse hold could be assigned a proportion of total calories that was attributable to each foodgroup @eq-food-groups-calorie-ratio.

Household information was then joined on household number ('hhno') to obtain the correct goverment office region for each household.

## Project scalability

The exact aggregation scripts that transform the raw diet diary data into usuable machine learning inputs are specific to the conventions of the 1974 to 2000 NFS data collection process. Ingestion of other similar dietary data would not automatically work with those scripts. 

That said, modifications to the ingestion and aggregation scripts could facilitate ingestion of applicable similar data. Once ingested and aggregated according to the feature engineering steps described above, harmonizable diet data from other sources (the UK in later years, the United States, or other countries) could be integrated into the analysis. 

The chronic disease data from the GBD Results tool is easily scalable, and compatible chronic disease SEV data for other developed nations could be obtained and integegrated into this analysis.



## Ethics and Responsible Use

The data is used under a non-commercial educational license, and comes both anonymized and pre-aggregated by the service providers to remove personally identifiable information (PII) and ensure confidentiality.
